title: Love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:9–18)
hookLine: leave the edges of the field for the poor; love your neighbor as yourself

lines: THE SICKLES STOP AT THE CORNERS.
cards: A farmer is bringing in the harvest. The sickles swing through the wheat, row after row, and when they reach the corners of the field, they stop. On purpose.
Behind them, a few stalks have fallen, and nobody goes back for them. In the vineyard, dropped grapes are left lying too. It looks like sloppy farming.
It's actually the law, right in the middle of Leviticus, between the sacrifices, the skin diseases and the priestly clothing.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest."
The grapes too: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God." It's welfare built into the field itself. The poor don't beg at the farmhouse door.
They walk in and gather what was left for them, with their own hands, with dignity. That's how Ruth, a poor foreign widow, ends up gleaning in the field of Boaz, a story the path reaches next year.
The Jewish oral law later gave a whole tractate of the Mishnah to these corners, called Peah, corner. Then chapter nineteen keeps going, all ordinary life. Don't hold back a worker's wages overnight.
"Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind." Don't spread gossip. Don't stand idle while your neighbor's life is in danger.
Don't hate your brother in your heart, take revenge or bear a grudge. And then, almost tucked in at the end: "but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD."
This is the line Jesus will quote as the second great commandment, straight from Leviticus. Look at the shape of the chapter. Love your neighbor isn't a warm feeling floating in the air.
It's corners of fields, wages paid on time, the deaf and the blind protected, grudges dropped.
Love has edges you can see.

teach.h: “THOU SHALT LOVE THY NEIGHBOUR AS THYSELF.”
teach.b: And later in the same chapter, the stranger among you is to be loved as yourself too.

how: Christians learn 'love thy neighbour as thyself' as the second great commandment, and some churches and farms practice modern gleaning, gathering leftover crops after harvest for food banks.

o: a tenth of the harvest given to the priests
the corner of the field left unreaped for the poor
a feast held when the last grain is gathered

games.q: what's inside Leviticus 19 — tap the pairs.
p: fallen stalks left on the ground
the line Jesus calls the second

s: love your neighbor as yourself first appears in the Gospels
it's Leviticus 19:18. Jesus quotes it as the second great commandment.
the law let the poor gather the field's corners themselves
they didn't beg at the door; they gleaned with their own hands.
it's wages, gossip, the deaf and the blind, grudges, and love.

games.q: you're a farmer bringing in the harvest. the sickles reach the corners of the field. what does the law say?
o: reap it all; you planted it.
stop, and leave the corners standing.
reap it and give a tenth to the priest.
games.why: leave the corners and the gleanings "for the poor and stranger". the field itself is built to feed people.

practice: Picture your own field: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, the last slice, the best seat.

Choose one corner where you could stop the sickle a little early and leave something standing, without making a speech about it, and picture someone else gathering it. If you pray, pray for whoever will.

wordCard.voice: Peah. Hebrew for corner, the Mishnah's name for the harvest law: leaving the edges of the field standing for the poor and the stranger.

orig.note: Hebrew: and you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

carryVoice: Your line: leave the edges. The field was built to feed more than the farmer. See you tomorrow.
